title: Audio Evaluation — WER, MOS, UTMOS, MMAU, FAD, and the Open Leaderboards
service: EvalSuite: normalized WER/CER scoring, a SQLite leaderboard with intervals and protocols, paired bootstrap comparisons, a streaming per-domain error-rate report and weighted suite scores

parts.lesson_anchor: ASR metrics: WER and CER; Use It rule 1 (normalize before scoring); code/main.py normalize and cer; quiz Q9 (contractions and numbers, expand before stripping punctuation) and Q10 (CER without normalization)
planted_bugs: the character path (CER) splits the raw text and skips normalize, as the lesson's cer() does, so a full-width digit and the ideographic full stop count as errors

normalize keeps the lesson's re.sub(r'[^a-z0-9\s]', '', text) after the Unicode punctuation table and deletes Han, kana, Cyrillic and accented letters; the failure surfaces two calls away, as a ValueError in error_counts about an empty reference
contractions are expanded after the punctuation table has turned the apostrophe into a space, so what's never matches
_punctuation_table rescans all 1,114,112 code points on every normalize call
parts.timing_assert: 24 scored pairs under 0.1 s (rebuilding the table costs about 46 ms per normalize call, 2.2 s for the 48 calls on an idle machine and up to 4.3 s under load; built once, about 0.2 ms)
parts.overfix_guard: the lesson's ASCII regex brought back for speed empties the Chinese reference; a [^\w\s] regex or an isalnum() filter turns Devanagari vowel signs into spaces, so किताबें and किताब become the same letters (must stay 1/4); ASCII string.punctuation or NFC instead of NFKC keeps the Japanese full stop or the full-width digit; NFKD accent stripping makes 'un café noir' match 'un cafe noir' (must stay 1/3); a letters-only filter drops digits (3号楼 against 5号楼 must stay 1/3); exempting the apostrophe from the punctuation pass leaves the quotes on 'yes'

deviations: Part 1: Chinese and Japanese are already routed to CER; the planted CER defect is the lesson code's own, cer() scoring the raw text (quiz Q10). Case, width and punctuation come with that bug, Unicode letters with the lesson's ASCII-only class, contractions with their order (quiz Q9). Numbers are spelled out by working code and asserted, which keeps Part 1 at four layers.
Part 1: the timing defect is a Unicode punctuation table rebuilt on every call. Edit distance stays correct because 06/04 already plants its exponential recursion.

Part 2: every entry also carries a protocol (the text normalizer behind a WER, the reference set behind a FAD), because the lesson asks to report the normalization rule and to compare FAD against one reference set; ranking mixed protocols raises. The upsert must keep a model's first-appearance place among ties, which rules out INSERT OR REPLACE; the model that appears first sorts last by name, so a tie-break by name fails as well. A worse re-run still replaces the result. The INSERT OR REPLACE trap is shared with 06/10's result store; what is new here is exact ranking of near-equal floats, metric direction and range, and protocol comparability.

Part 3: percentile_interval is a separately tested helper with a fixed rule, so the index and the 1 - 0.9 rounding traps are exact. The bootstrap itself is checked through properties that hold for any way of drawing from random.Random(seed) (checked over 300 seeds and four draw methods), not through hard-coded draws.

Part 4: the wire format is CSV (06/03 uses NDJSON, 06/04 and 06/09 SSE, 06/06 RTTM). A report is due every N utterances rather than per batch, so the output does not depend on batching, and a pooled '*' row sits next to the per-domain rows.

Part 5: a metric leaf reads the result of its parent subset and is mapped onto 0..1 with the metric's worst and best values in METRICS, the same table Part 2 ranks with. A weight-0 child is reported but not counted.
